projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ralph L. Jessop was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Ralph L. Jessop. Mr. Jessop served in the U.S. Army with the 7th Division. He served in Hawaii and the Aleutians, and his highest rank was staff sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at the home of Mr. Jessop's daughter in Concord Township, Ohio, on December 23rd, 2002. Ralph was 83 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Where was I living in 1941? Bellefonte, Pennsylvania --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- and which was about 15 miles from where -- isn't it?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: No. 1941, honey, you were in the service.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah. 1941. I went in the service in 1939.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In 1939? All right. You enlisted?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. I enlisted. And I went to Hawaii. I was in the of 64th Anti-Aircraft in, in Hawaii. I was over there a little over two years. And then that was foreign service then which was then is, it's not now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And they -- you could stay two years foreign service or you could stay your third year over there if you wanted to, and they called me in the office and asked me if I wanted to extend my third year. I says: "I don't think so." I says: "I think I'm going stateside for a while first," and 'cause when -- we were sleeping with loaded rifles and fixed bayonets over in Hawaii. We knew it was coming. Back here, I don't -- I'm not too sure but we, we knew it was coming. We knew Hawaii was gonna be invaded, and they called me in and says: "Would you like to extend your third year over here?" I said: "I don't think so." I says, "I think I want to go stateside for a while first." And I got as far as California when Pearl Harbor was hit. And we had about, I think about 85 percent casualties over there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you stationed when you were in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: At Fort Shafter.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: At Fort Shafter? Okay.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. And our maneuver position, our wartime position was Pearl Harbor. And it came like this, you know, and we were right on the beach in Pearl Harbor, that's where -- and that's where they hit. That's where the Arizona was sunk, and all those ships. And so I says: "No," I says. "I think I'm going home for a while." I never got any further than California. (Laughter.) So that's where I was when Pearl Harbor was hit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And I talked to a couple guys that survived that. Then I think -- I don't know how long it was before I got home. It was over almost fours years, I think, before I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any close friends at Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Quite a few. Quite a few. And, yeah, 'cause they, they were right on the beach in Pearl Harbor, and they got, they got the heck kicked out of 'em. So I -- it's not, not being a coward, but I think I made the right choice when I come back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: But I wanted to go to go home for a while first 'cause we knew the war was coming. I got as far as California and that, that was it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And then what did they do with you?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, I took -- we was on the corner of Carson Street and Cherry in Long Beach, California. I was at Anti-Aircraft, millimeters, and we protected that until we got the call to go overseas again. And we were supposed to go to the South Pacific, so they issued us Sun Tans, you know, for the South Pacific. We ended up going up to the Aleutian Islands. And what they gave us to go up there was that we had lined pants and a lined field jacket, no more than what you'd wear around here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And we have an awful lot of casualties up there from frost bite. I seen guys take their socks off and pull the skin right off with their socks. It was terrible. And it was just a -- well, on an island like that, it was a damp cold, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And so these were from Pennsylvania. I got the guys to wear a pair of socks, put their shoes on, put a pair of socks over their shoes and put their Arctics on. The guys that did that didn't get any frost bite.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: There was a lot, lot of guys lost their feet up there. Yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go to the Aleutians?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: When was that? 1943. 1943. That's a long time ago. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Had the Japanese already invaded at that point?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. They had, Attu, and they had, they had Shemya.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They had Shemya?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Two islands almost side by side. So we landed on Attu and we were fortunate. We had a beachhead established before they knew we were there, and so we took the, we cleaned the Japanese out of Attu.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And I'll tell you one thing. Those Japanese were vicious fighters. And we cleaned them out of Attu, then we left there and we went to Shemya. And they evidently knew we were coming 'cause we got, we landed on Shemya. The only thing we found was a couple little campfires going. They must have just have left there so there was no Japanese on Shemya at all. So we, we stayed on Shemya till my tour was over up the Aleutians, then they sent me back, back to go to school. And so that was the end of my Aleutian campaign.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of combat on Attu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: First day of combat when you went into Attu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. We --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: We landed in landing barges, you know. And we had, pretty well had a beachhead established before they knew we were there. I could never understand that 'cause there was a lot of Japanese on Attu. And we pretty well cleaned 'em out up there. And I know one -- there was a cave up there on Attu and that's where their headquarters were, and we blocked that thing and I imagine there is still some of 'em in there. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: That's where you got your bronze star.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me how you earned your bronze star.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, they had a breakthrough up there one night. They broke through our, our ranks, the infantry ranks. We'd have an ammunition dump, and that's what they were after 'cause they, their rifles fired .31 caliber. Ours were .30 caliber. Now, they could fire ours but we couldn't fire theirs. We had some of their shells. They could go in our rifle chamber only about that far.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: So they were after our ammunition dump. And we went up and, and blocked that, you know, and, and we, we -- well, out of my platoon, I had one killed, seven wounded, and we killed, well, I don't know, 35, 40 Japanese that night. Those didn't -- they acted like they didn't have the training that we had. We had -- like I was a platoon sergeant. We went up there. And we had a change of command, you know. Something happened to me, someone else would take over, but they didn't have that. Once they lost their leadership, they were done. They didn't know what to do. That was to our advantage. Yuh. And their grenades. Our grenades would blow you to pieces. They -- I was in a foxhole up there one night. I looked down and here was -- one of their grenades was laying between my feet. I just took my heels and tramped it down in the muskeg. It went off and it didn't bother me any. And they had a percussion cap under it. It was a grenade. What they would take, they would take, hit it on their helmet and detonate it and then throw it. But they didn't -- there, there was only like a big firecracker. But when one of ours went off, it would blow you to pieces. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So their grenades did not have shrapnel, is that what it was?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No. They didn't have the shrapnel like, you know, our grenades were, of course, corrugated, you know. When they went off, they were all over the place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And then, no, theirs weren't like that. Our, our equipment was far superior to what theirs were.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: That where they got drunk on sake?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's here about that.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, they had, they had a breakthrough up there one night, and they came down off of those hills and they were all drunk on sake. And that was a mistake. When they did that, they didn't have a chance. They were -- I don't think there was any of them got down into the beach alive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Falling down the hill or something?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were they falling down the hill or something?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No. Well, I guess they did it for courage or -- I don't know, but they were fanatics. They -- I'd, I always thought they didn't use a lot of military sense, you know. We, we did. We had chain of command. And once the leader got shot, something like that, then we had a chain of command which they didn't have. Once they lost their leadership, they were done and they were scattered all over the place. And I know there was a lieut -- there was a Lieutenant Hammer was, we went up to stop the breakthrough one night, and I looked over. Lieutenant Hammer kept on going like that to me, and I looked around and I didn't see anything. About as from as from here to the piano there was foxhole, and they dug their foxholes down then back under and you could run past their foxholes and you couldn't see anything. They'd be back under there. Didn't take us long to get wise to that. So we'd pass the foxhole where we'd reach down there and take a grenade and throw it back in underneath there. (Laughter.) So, so that, that was a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can remember about Attu? I haven't heard anything about this before.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: On Attu?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Anything else you can tell me?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What about your cold shower?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What about your cold shower?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, boy. Up there, I don't know. We were up there about two months before we even had a shower.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I'm glad I wasn't there.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And another guy and I, we took our rifles and a towel. There was a waterfall coming down off the mountain, and you know how cold it is. I says: "Come on," I says. "We're gonna take a shower." I says: "You stand guard while I take one. I'll stand guard while you took one. And we got back underneath that water fall and took a shower. Boy, was that cold. (Laughter.) It was a little pond, you know, where it come down off the, off the mountain, and I, I, I undressed, and I had my winter underwear with me and, and I says: "I'll go first." So I undressed and he stood guard and I jumped in that doggone pond, and, boy, was that cold. Felt ice around there. (Laughter.) it's a wonder we didn't catch a death out there.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You still didn't tell 'em why you got your bronze star.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You got a hole through your rain suit.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's hear about that --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: We, we stopped --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- particularly about how you got your bronze star.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. We stopped a rain -- my platoon went up and stopped a breakthrough one night and I, all I got -- we had rain suits on --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- and I thought I lost my left leg. I had, about right in there I had about three or four holes, rifle holes right through my rain suit. Never touched my leg and, oh, it was enough to knock you down. I was afraid to look. (Laughter.) I said: "Oh, boy." I was afraid to look but I survived it. I'd never want to do it again, not in that place anyway. We used to -- up there we pitied the guys they were down in the South Pacific in the jungles. The jungles, you know, they had not only the Japanese to fight, they had snakes and everything else, but we didn't have anything like that up there. All we had to worry about was the Japanese. And we took, we took two prisoners, and we took 'em over -- another guy and I took 'em over pancakes and syrup. They never heard of that stuff before. We took 'em over to -- they had a cage built. They had 'em in there. We took 'em over and gave them a hot cakes and syrup, you know, and they'd take the hot cakes and roll 'em up and eat 'em and then drink the syrup. (Laughter.) And they weren't as equipped as well as we were. We had leggings, you know, we could wear. And their leggings was like World War I guys wore, you know. They'd wrap 'em around their legs. That's just what they had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: So they weren't near as well equipped as we were. And their rifles were, a lot of 'em were just .25 caliber, .25 and then .31. I know I had a carbine. I was a platoon leader and I had a carbine. I had ammunition, M-1 ammunition scattered all over the place, but there was no, none, no ammunition there for a carbine, so I got up there in the hill. I took the bolt out of my carbine and threw that and went and took my rifle and threw it that way. And there was guy laying there that had been killed, and I picked up his M-1 and then I picked up a couple bandoliers of ammunition and hung it across my shoulder. Then after the battle was over, they inventoried the, the equipment, you know, and the guy says, he says: "Where's your carbine?" I says: "Up there in the hills somewhere." He says: "Well, you'll have to pay for it." I says: "Don't give me that horseshit." I says: "That was a combat zone. You don't pay for anything in a combat zone." (Laughter.) That's exactly what I told him. I says: "You don't pay for anything in a combat zone." So I had that M-1 until I come back to the states. Then they sent me back to the states. I went down to Fort Benning, Georgia. I went to officers' training school. I was in training, training school down there. And all of a sudden they cancelled everything. So I went from officers' training school into the field artillery and that's what I was doing when the war ended.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And I was enlisted. And when the war ended, you had so many points, you know. I had, I think, 180 points. They were leaving guys out with less than a hundred points. So I went over to battalion headquarters and I says, I says: "How come I'm not getting outta here?" And they dug out my service record and someone had written across my service record with a red grease pencil: "Desires to stay in military service." I says: "If I knew who that was, I'd go break his doggone neck" (laughter) 'cause I wanted to go home. I had a, I'd had enough. So the guy says: "Do you really want to get outta here?" And I says -- I was regular army. They thought I was gonna stay. And he says: "You really want to get outta here?" I says: "Yes, I do." He says, he says: "Well, I'll take care of that." He says: "I'll have you out of here tomorrow." So the next day I was on my way home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you in the Aleutians?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I guess about 18 months, two years, something like that.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You had been in Pearl Harbor right before the attack.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's what he was saying, yes.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He just got stateside.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you married at the time when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting letters from home, packages, that sort of thing, from your family?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I remember one package I got, and it was mailed in July and it caught up with me in January. And it was a box. And I opened it up and it was homemade cookies and fudge, and it was all --

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: And an apple.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And an apple. The only thing left in there was the apple core and a bunch of crumbs. (Laughter.) I wrote home and told my mother. I says: "Boy." I told her how good it was, and she never knew any different. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What about the present she sent you for Christmas when you were in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: When I was over in Hawaii, she sent me -- my mom, I guess she thought the climate through the world was all the same. When I was over in Hawaii, I got a Christmas present from her. It was a scarf. (Laughter.) I never told her any different.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: She must have known what was coming.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: She couldn't believe that like the Hawaii the climate was almost the same all year around. They had their winter months over there but all we did was change shirts from khaki to wool shirts, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: We had some chilly times over there but nothing like we get around here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was life like in Hawaii then before the attack on Pearl Harbor? What was it like there in Honolulu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, it was, it was pretty nice. We -- I was in Anti-Aircraft and we, we used to go out to Nanaculi (ph) Beach. That's where we had target practice. They'd send a plane up and two in a sleeve, you know, with the fire power. When I first went over, we we had three-inch guns. Then they got rid of those and got 90 millimeters, and we'd go out there and then we'd -- I was in charge of the computer section, which we controlled the guns. We'd put the guns on remote control, then with the computer we had, my crew would operate the computer. We'd track a sleeve, you know, then the guns would follow right along. We blew many a one out of the sky. (Laughter.) Yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how soon or how close to the attack was it when you left and came back to the States?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: How what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How close was it? When, when did you leave Hawaii and come back to the states for that short time?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, I was over there, what, about two and-a-half years, I think.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I guess I'm trying to, I'm trying to phrase this properly. How close to that, to the attack on Pearl Harbor was that when you left?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I got as far as California.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I know.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: When?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Timewise do you --

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Timewise was it a a week or what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A week or so before the attack you left Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Now you're taxing my memory.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I was trying to figure out how close it was to the time that they actually attacked.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, we -- it took us, I think, almost -- no, about 15 days to go from Hawaii to the west coast --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- and I was in Camp Long, California, when Pearl Harbor was hit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you think you might have left maybe two or three weeks before the attack? In November of '41?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And our outfit was right at Pearl City.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Anti-Aircraft. And it wasn't too many of 'em left.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: So I often thought the good Lord was on my side 'cause I made the right decision anyway. (Laughter.) Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Getting back to Attu, how many Japanese were on Attu --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- roughly, do you know?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: There was a couple thousand on there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Couple thousand?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that, they were all from Kiska, right?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: On the island of Kiska?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: They were on there too, but we took Attu back from the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Then they moved our outfit to Kiska and -- to do the same thing. When we got to Kiska, there's a wood fire burning on the beach but there was nobody on the island, so we figured they had just left Kiska when we landed on there. We landed in barges, you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- and we went through all over the island. Wasn't a Jap on that Kiska, but Attu was a different story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memories of Attu that we didn't cover?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, I don't know. We took a, we took a few prisoners and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, did they, they just give up? I mean the stories are that the Japanese didn't want to be taken prisoner.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, they didn't. A lot of 'em committed suicide when they knew they were gonna be captured or, or shot, you know. They had an awful lot of Japanese committed suicide. They were taught that and we weren't. And you'd be surprised. There was a cave up there how many Japanese went in there. They did commit suicide 'cause that, that's what they were taught. They were taught if they were captured, they would be tortured. And I guess we were the other way around. We didn't give a damm. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: How did you treat your prisoners?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: How did you treat your prisoners?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, heck. I think the guys, they were way ahead when they were captured and, of course, we gave 'em hotcakes and syrup and everything we had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And I think we made friends with 'em, with the prisoners we had. But they, they seemed to relax. They were scared to death when we, you know, when we first got them. They thought they'd be tortured. They were taught that. But they, they were eventually sent back to Japan.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What about the night you hit your own ammunition dump?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What about the night you hit your own ammunition dump?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh. (Laughter.) We had, we had an ammunition dump up there, and I forget how we got that thing started. Holy smokes. It was like the Fourth of July. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You hit your own ammunition dump, though?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You hit your own ammunition dump?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: With the anti-aircraft?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: With your own and anti-aircraft?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No. No. With the infantry. When we landed up there, my platoon went in as infantry --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Okay.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- because the muskeg up there, we -- those was 90-millimeter guns, they'd sink right down there and you couldn't move 'em and so we went in as infantry. We hit an ammunition dump up there and, holy smokes, there was -- you laid flat on the ground and 'cause it was just like the Fourth of July. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you think you were hitting an enemy's ammunition dump or was it just a mistake?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: It was a mistake. Yuh, it was a mistake. It was, was going through what -- I had the bayonet on my rifle and there was a couple pup tents were pitched in there and, and I'd take my bayonet and we'd rip the pup tents open. One guy was ready to shoot, and I pushed his rifle aside. I says: "That's a GI." It was a GI that had crawled in. He was wounded in the leg and he had crawled in there to hide, you know. And he'd been in there two or three days and we pulled him out. He had gangrene in his one leg. It was -- my gosh, it was like that. So we got him out and got him back on the ship hospital, a hospital ship, and I know they had to take his leg off up here somewhere because it was -- I don't see how they could have, could save it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You have memories of buddies on Attu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Of what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Buddies on Attu.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Buddies?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yuh.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: They still had reunions up to what, two years ago?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. We had reunions up to two years ago.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Up to two years ago you had a reunion with your buddies.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What are the type of things did you guys do for entertainment to relieve the tension?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, there for a long time we didn't have any. Then after the combat was over, then -- who was it? Was it -- Bob Hope come up.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You played cards a lot.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yuh. We played poker a lot. And Bob Hope come up. And who else was it? It was Red Skeleton. They come up with a USO troupe, and they put on a pretty good program for us then. Relieved the tension, I'll tell you. That, that was nice. I got a kick out of the guys up there. That's the first time they seen a female in about 18 months. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And how did they react to that?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, normally. (Laughter.) Yuh. They come up with a few USO shows when we were up there. And we built a, they built a theater up there and it was, it was pretty nice for up there. They put a stage on it, you know. And I don't know if you remember Bill Bendix or not. He was a, he was part of the show. He was pretty good. But they'd, they'd come up with the USO shows, you know. A lot of movie stars would come up there. Loretta Young was one of 'em.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: She, she come up there, and I forget who the other ones up there were but they put on a nice show for us.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What did you eat when you were in combat?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: C rations.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Describe that.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, when we were in combat, they had little packages done up like that, and inside there was a couple crackers and some kind of almost like hardtack. That's what you carried with you. I had, I had three of 'em in my pack. When you got hungry, you'd just go out and take a couple bites and put it back.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What's hardtack?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What is hardtack?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: A hard bread, a hard piece of bread?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. It's combat. That's food compressed, you might say what it was.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You had chocolate?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, chocolate. They'd give you a big thing of solid chocolate, you know. And that one night when you had a breakthrough up there, I had a big piece of that and stuffed inside of my face. I said: "What am I doing with that in there? If I got shot, I'd probably choke to death." So I spit it out. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How often did you get hot meals in?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, not very often. We didn't get any till, till the combat was over. Then I had to give our cooks credit because they couldn't get any food in to us. That was, the sea was rough. They couldn't get any food in to us. So what they had up there, they'd take whatever they had and they'd, they would make hot dogs out of it. They'd make meat loaf out of it. Boy, they deserved a medal 'cause they kept us going because they, those can rations, you know, C rations, K rations and all that stuff, they'd take that and make meat loaf out of it and, yeah, they did. Boy, they deserved a medal, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, given the weather up there in the Aleutians, was there a problem with depression with the guys?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yuh. That, that was terrible. Like I said before, when we landed on there, we didn't have any more than what you'd wear around here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Field -- lined field jackets, you know. Winter underwear that wasn't near enough up there. So after the combat was over, then they came in with parkas, you know, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- I had some pictures at home but I was wearing my parkas and, and combat boots, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: After the action, was there cabin fever with the guys with nothing to do?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, pretty much, yeah. I think we had quite a few poker games.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That kept you busy.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: (Laughter.) I remember one night we had, we stopped a breakthrough. Boy, it was cold that night. And I had a guy on my section. His name was Brownie. And I mean we had a stop watch and we kept passing it from one guy to another, you know, and I -- well, it was cold enough that we, about every 15 minutes we changed from one guy to another, you know. And this one guy -- Borgan (ph) was his name -- he had, he had the stop watch in his hands, and he was going like that and he was looking for Brownie to pass the watch over to him, and he says: "Where's that Brownie? Where's that goddamn Brownie?" And he was, he was -- I couldn't help but laugh that night. (Laughter.) We were down in a place called Sarana (ph) Pass and we were heading that off because the Japanese were coming from the other side up that pass. When they come up through the pass, then we'd pick 'em off. So that didn't last very long. I never forget when that guy's going, Borgan's going: "Where is that Brownie? Where's that goddamn Brownie? (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: And now Borgan's dead but Brownie's still in --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I don't know how many of them are gone now. There's quite a few out of that bunch that are gone.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies when you were on Attu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. Yeah. Well, that one night up there, I had one killed and seven wounded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: One guy I pitied the most. He was a swimming instructor at Michigan State, and Eddie Dupus (ph). And he got hit here right up through his arm, come out his shoulder, and they had to take his arm completely off. That didn't go too good with a swimming instructor. He was a nice guy.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I know you told him about your rain coat, but did you tell him about the men on both sides that night?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had a captain on this side and a major on this side, and I was in the center. And we had -- the Japanese were, we were pretty well bottled up. It was just a matter of time. And this major says: "Come on. Let's go get 'em. Let's go get 'em." And the captain's the same way. I says: "Why?" I says: "You're only gonna have more casualties." I says, "Wait 'em out." And, well, first thing I know this guy got killed, the captain got killed, and I was in the middle. All I got was a couple holes through my rain suit. And that, that was -- they got killed. And to this day it, it was foolish. They didn't have to do that 'cause we had 'em all bottled up; that they said: "Come on. Let's go. Let's go." And I says: "Why." And we'd -- so both those guys got killed. Kind of foolish. Oh, they were supposed to be leaders but that, they didn't have to do that.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Were they all pretty young?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Were they all pretty young?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You had to be young with no gut, no guts to do that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Or guts and no brains.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: That's it. Guts and no brains. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, I, I don't know. They -- it's been so long ago you don't think much of it anymore, but yeah. We had -- I think what I, what I hated up there when the, when the combat was over, they had an affay (ph) trailer they pulled with their Cat, you know. And they'd go around gathering up bodies, you know. And out of my platoon I had a guy's name of Smallires (ph). He was, he was shot once beside the nose and once in the chest. I kept going -- when they were gathering up the bodies, I kept going up 'cause he was missing. I was going up and I went up until I found him, and then I, I didn't go up anymore but they were going around gathering up bodies. And they had a cemetery up there they called the Little Falls Cemetery, and they would take a bulldozer and they'd dig a great big ditch, and down at the bottom of the ditch about every, every four or five feet, then they'd dig graves, you know. They'd lay the, take the bodies, wrap 'em in a blanket, put binder twine around their neck, around their waist and around their feet and lay 'em down there and then take a bulldozer and then covered them up. Then they had little white crosses, you know. And to this day I don't know how they'd take a bulldozer, you know, and cover them all up, and how they knew that they didn't move bodies, I don't know. It didn't make any difference anyhow but they put white crosses, you know, up there.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I wonder if they're still there.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, I would imagine. I often thought I'd like to go back up sometime.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I'll send you.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I'll send you.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: All right. I would, though. I'd like to go back up there sometime. They, they called it the Little Falls Cemetery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And they had little white crosses made for each when someone died up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that was in the Aleutians?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that on Attu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Attu, yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I wonder if that's still there.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I wonder if that's still there.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I would assume.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I would --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I mean I think the families can request that the bodies be brought back but, but many of them would, you know, not do that.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, I -- if they'd asked for bodies to be brought back, they were sent back --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- if they could, you know, if they were in any condition to be sent. They did do that. I know they did do that. But they called that the Little Falls Cemetery. And they had, they had built an archway over the entrance to the cemetery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And they had on there Little Falls, and it was, it was pretty impressive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Any of you have any questions from stories that I haven't, that I don't know about?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: We should because we've heard so many.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: We used to stay up at night. When we went home to see him, he'd tell us stories.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I think you covered it very well, though.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I think you covered it very well.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, probably.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's good. I'll take your word for it. Because that happens a lot of time, you know. I don't know about your specific stories so I can ask you general questions but I can't --

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: It's hard as you sit here because he, I'm sure he has lots more but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: -- but just to think of 'em all at once --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: -- it's hard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's why I keep the tape recorder running now, when you do think of other stuff, if you think of anything, speak up. It's still running.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've got some forms for the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, we moved from -- after the battle of Attu was over, then our outfit moved from Attu to Shemya, which was just about 40 miles. We set up anti-aircraft defense over there, then we built still runways for planes to come in and land. The planes that were on there, then they'd were pretty close to Japan, then they they'd take off from there then go bomb the islands over in Japan. So we, we had a nice time building runways.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And those were B-29s taking off from Shemya?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: B-29s and B-26s.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Mm-hmm. And they had a lot of B-38s up there, fighter planes up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I know one night there was a, a fighter plane come in. They had pretty steep mountains up there. And this fighter, this B-38 come in, you know, has the twin booms in the back. They come in and and they didn't cut quick enough and he hit the top of, of that mountain. That thing just flew to pieces.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You told me there was a woman behind every tree but there weren't any trees. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I told her: "Boy, I liked it up there." I says, "There was a woman behind every tree but there was no trees." (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you obviously were dating at the time, right, but not married?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I was too young. I wasn't allowed.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I think the first time I dated her I think she was 13, right?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Fifteen. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: A long time ago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were stateside on -- were you stateside on V-E Day in May of '45?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And then also you were still in the army and stateside on V-J Day?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I was down in Fort Benning, Georgia, when V-E Day. Boy, did we ever celebrate. We went to town and got drunk. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, we, we really celebrated when V-E Day come through. That was something. We knew everything was just about over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: He was home. And he says, "If I'm more than halfway back, I'll have to go. If I'm not halfway back, I'll come back." And he was more than halfway when, in fact, he was in Columbus, Georgia.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I mean Ohio.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yuh.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Stayed in the dorms there.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, I went down to Fort Benning going to, going to school.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: But when the armistice was signed.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And I would, I come home on a furlough. I hadn't been home in a long time. I come home on furlough after the war ended, and I had to go back down to Fort Benning, Georgia. I said: "I'll tell you what," I says. "If I'm not halfway on my way down and the war ends, I'll come back. I was in Columbus, Ohio, when we got word that the war had ended.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So this would be right after they dropped the second bomb then?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yuh. What did you think when you heard about them dropping the bomb?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I think I was in California.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you comprehend what that was?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Could you comprehend what an atomic bomb was?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: We knew what it was, yeah. We knew if they had dropped a couple of those, that was it. I'm glad we had 'em first. Boy, that was, that was something. Boy. That atomic bomb, hmm. I'd hate to see another war start now. If they had another war right now, we'd get it right here, debris all over the place. One thing about the Japanese. Once their leaders were shot, they didn't have the control, the command and control like we did. I was a platoon sergeant. If anything would have happened to me, then they were going down another chain, you know, on down. They didn't have that. Once they lost their leadership, they were done.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: They didn't know what to do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: They, they'd come down off those hills and yelling: "Blood for Tojo. Blood for Tojo. Kill Roosevelt. Kill Roosevelt."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. Just as plain as English as you and I had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The only English they knew.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. "Blood for Tojo. Kill Roosevelt. Kill Roosevelt."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And so were you dealing with a lot of banzai attacks on Attu?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: A couple, yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. They were fanatics --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- because they, they thought it was an honor to die in battle. Us American GIs were the other way around. We wanted to save our lives --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- and kill them. Yuh. They, they thought it was an honor to die in battle. And we, we only had a couple prisoners out of that whole batch. I was in the reserves then. And that was a mistake, I think, 'cause they called me back in and I went down to Fort Meade, Maryland, and while I was down there, then they -- I got orders to go overseas, and I was in transit and I had her and three kids, and if you had more than two dependents, they weren't supposed to take you. And they had me raise the ship out, you know, and I went down to headquarters. First, I come home and got my car. I went down so I could go different places, you know. (END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.)

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And then I got ahold of my orders and I, they had me raise the, ready to ship out and I got ahold of my home orders and -- I says: "Unh-unh." I says: "Nope." I said: "If I get" -- I was supposed to go down to Kentucky. And I says: "If I go to Kentucky, these orders will never catch up with me."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: So I grabbed my orders and I hand-carried them everywhere I was supposed to go. And in two days I was on my way home. I says: "No."

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Daddy's baby heading back. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He made a few mistakes with the paperwork. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: She'd turned it all out of bed and I'd put it back. No, daddy. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't want to record any home front memories, huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't want to record any memories from your home?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: No. That's fine. I think he did a very good job, though, what he was doing.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: I tell you, we was very proud of him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I was going down to, I was going to -- I come back. I was going to school down at Fort Benning, and the captain called me in the office and, and I didn't know what he called me in for. And he says: "Do you know you're getting a citation?" I said: "No." I said: "No, I didn't know anything about it." And, boy. I started wishing my mom and dad was there, down there. They had had a big parade, you know. The whole outfit had a parade. I was standing there with the commanding general and I got the bronze star.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's when you got the bronze star?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: They gave me the bronze star. I says, oh, I wish my mom and dad would have been there. That was a big day.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: And how old were you then?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, in my twenties somewhere.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: About 25.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: About 25.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I don't, I don't believe I could do that again. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You'd have to work out a little bit. Let's hope no one has to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes, exactly. You think we got it all?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you think we got it all?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I think so. I often wondered when we were up in the Aleutians why they didn't shake those darn islands and let the Japanese have 'em, one or the other.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. They really had to stop them from moving any farther from where they were --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As long as they could stop 'em, then that was --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: That was their idea. That was their stepping stone to Alaska.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And they would -- Attu was closer to Japan than it was the United States.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And they'd attack going to Attu, Shemya, and Adak right on back through into Alaska and that's what their idea was so we stopped them on Attu.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were they going for -- was the plan to get Alaskan oil perhaps or --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- or were they trying to take over Canada?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No. I think they had an idea they were gonna get into Alaska and come down through to California.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And I'm glad they just didn't get that far. When I was in California, I was on, we were on the beach. I was in Anti-Aircraft. We were on the beach. And they got close enough that they shelled California. They shelled -- a lot of guys never knew that but they did. And they'd get their submarines in pretty close, you know, then they'd shell the west coast, but they didn't do it very often but they did it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they shell Long Beach, in that area?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Yuh. They'd get their submarines in there, and the submarines never got away. They got sunk before they got out of the harbor. I, I don't know why they ever got in that close. I know they'd never get out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'd heard about attacks from Santa Barbara, but I didn't realize they'd shot the Long Beach area.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. They'd come in pretty close. I was stationed at Long Beach. I don't remember how long. I liked Long Beach.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's nice.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I used to live out in California.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I used to hitchhike up to Holly, Hollywood.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: And he danced with movie stars.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh. Did you go to the Hollywood Canteen?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Hey, that was nice, that Hollywood Canteen. You'd go in there, they had everything you wanted to eat. And the whole thing was run by movie stars. And the one thing -- I remember Myrna Loy. She was always my, she was always my favorite movie star, but her legs were about like that.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Oh. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you dance with her?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you dance with her?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I danced with a lot of 'em. I danced with Hedy LaMarr.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Deanna Durbin.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. Deanna Durbin. Oh, a bunch of stars. They'd come around and they -- you wouldn't grab them. They'd grab you. That was at the Hollywood Canteen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And that was, that was a nice place. All kind of movie stars in there.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: How were you treated when you got back home? You know, they treated the Vietnam vets so bad. How were you treated?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Better than the Vietnam vets.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I -- in California, you couldn't do anything out there. They would do it for you. I was disappointed when I come back to Pennsylvania. I thought, heck, they didn't even know there was a war going on back here. I was really disappointed when I come home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: But California you couldn't do anything. If -- we'd go out Long Beach Boulevard out there, we wanted to go to Hollywood, about the first car pass you would stop and pick you up and take you right where you wanted to go. Back here I got, I come into Altoona, and I lived in Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, then. And it took me almost all night to get home. No one stopped to pick you up. And I was -- I -- in fact, the next day when I got home, I went down to the local paper and I put an article in the paper about it.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Did you have your uiniform on?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Did you have your uniform on?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yes. But nobody here in, in Pennsylvania -- I thought: Boy. They just don't give a damn whether there was a war going on or not. That kind of made me mad, and I put an article in the paper about it.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: His mom didn't know he was coming. He threw stones at her bedroom window to wake her up.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. I, I come in and I was getting a little stone and I would throw 'em. My dad was never a very excitable person, and I threw stones at the bedroom window. And what did I yell out there?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: "Mrs.Jessop, your cow's arrived."

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I says: "Hey, Mrs. Jessop," I says, "your cow's arrived. Finally I heard her say: "That sounds like Ralph down there." That's the first time I ever saw my dad beat her down the steps. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. Did you have a nice celebration then when you got --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. All my brothers and sisters come home.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: You had a brother in the service too.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. My brother Sam was over in Guam. So right now I'm the only one left in our family out of eight. We had eight. My mom had eight kids, and Eddie was my oldest brother. He was old enough to be my dad before I was born. I was born in 1919.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So he would have been too old for World War II probably, right?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. He was very disappointed they wouldn't take him. He tried to enlist. He was too old.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was he too young for World War I?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He was too young?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: What about your dad? Was he in World War I?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: No. No. Dad was never in the service. My dad was -- we lived in Pennsylvania and they had a penitentiary there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And they had, they used to have horses and they don't have 'em anymore, but my dad was in charge of the horse barns. And, boy, those horses were beautiful. And the prisoners had a lot of pride in their teams, you know. They had the harnesses all dressed up. Boy, they were beautiful. My dad used to get great big bags of peanuts with the shells on, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: You weren't supposed to do it but he did it anyhow. He'd take a whole great big bag like that of peanuts with the shells on 'em, go up and put 'em in one of the mangers with the horses up there, you know, and for the prisoners, you know. You weren't supposed to do that but he did that. They'd go in there and put peanuts in their pockets. (Laughter.) But you can tell them for me on Attu if they want to, it's all right with me if they sink it. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No use for Attu?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: No. We threatened to send him there when he retired.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yuh. Lovely.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, that's been behind me for a good many years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, we're talking 60 years now since you went there probably. You went there in '43?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Went in the service in '39.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I was on -- when I come back, and I was down in Fort Benning, Georgia --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: -- they called me down there, and the guys that got citations, you know, and they called me in, and I was on Fort Benning On The Air.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yuh?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yeah. I was on about a half an hour down there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, great. When was that?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Nineteen forty --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right when you got back? Was that right when you got back or?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: After I got back, yuh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow. Very good.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. Anybody that had a, got a citation, they had him on the air.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: On the radio? That's great.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: It was called Fort Benning On The Air.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Well, you were at one time gonna go in to fly airplanes, weren't you? Your, your buddy went and you didn't. He was killed.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Para-troopers.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Para-troopers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. He, they formed the paratroopers when I first went in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: And this friend of mine, he says: "Come on," he says. "Let's, let's join the paratroopers." And I thought about it a little bit. And I says: "I don't think so." He says: "Why?" I says: "The first guys that join the paratroopers now are really gonna get it." And -- "No," he says. "We'll be, we'll be training paratroopers." I said, "I don't think so." So he went and I didn't. And he was killed over Sicily. He jumped over Sicily and that's where he was killed. He was a real good friend. He was from Evenmore, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There was a lot of guys were talked into the extra $50 a month and thought that was a good deal.

sp.speaker: Female Speaker
sp.p: Yuh.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: You got a little bit extra but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Yuh. That was too soon. That was the first -- well, the guys that joined the paratroopers, I'll tell you wasn't too many of 'em left. Well, a lot of 'em never even hit the ground alive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I thought: Why swing around up there in a parachute and someone shooting at me. I'd rather go on the ground where I had a chance.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Exactly. Yeah. Well, very good. You think we've got it now?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Well, the Aleutians was no picnic. It was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: It was chilly up there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, I'm amazed. Like I said, I talked to this other guy on Friday, and I would think depression would be a bigger problem with the weather and with the six hours of daylight certain times of the year and, you know, that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You guys kept busy playing cards?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: We were up there -- wintertime up there you only had a couple hours of daylight.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yuh, I know. And it's --

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: The summer was the other way around. We'd be out out playing ball 12:00 o'clock at night.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Yeah. I would think that would drive you nuts.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I'm not sure it didn't. (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you're still here. All right. Before I shut off the tape recorder, you think you've covered it?

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Ralph L. Jessop
sp.p: I thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.
(END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.)
